description: We are a motivated STEM team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are passionate about space exploration, science, technology, and innovation. Our goal is to develop a creative, practical solution using NASA's open data. We value teamwork, creativity, and problem-solving. We are looking for enthusiastic members with skills in coding, web development, graphic design, scientific research, and data analysis who are ready to collaborate and learn.
summary: Space Archive: The Little Explorer is an action-adventure 3D game about space exploration with a storyline that allows children and people interested in space to get acquainted with the robots left behind on other planets by humans. Users start the game by taking off from Earth, moving through the Solar System with the help of artificial intelligence named ORBIT, and landing the ship in a cinematic way at the Moon, Mars, and Titan. On the ground, the users move around in true gravity, visit 15 robots represented by 3D models, listen to their story, see a video explaining their mission, and give an answer to a question checking whether they got the information right. The list of robots includes Apollo 11's Lunar Module, Lunar Roving Vehicle, Surveyor, Sojourner, Ingenuity, Opportunity, Curiosity, InSight, Phoenix, Venera 13, Magellan, Vega balloons, Galileo probe, Cassini and Huygens. Every robot has a corresponding label – lander, rover, orbiter, flyby, or atmospheric probe. This solution is able to solve the problem by turning long technical articles into adventure and giving the connection between the design and discoveries of the machines.
details:
How it works and what it does. Space Archive: The Little Explorer is an online 3D game using a web browser. The player launches a rocket from Earth and then guides their spacecraft to each destination along the shortened route through the Solar System, controlling it by the keyboard or a touch stick. At the Moon, Mars and Titan, the game automatically plays a cinematic landing scene, then the player walks and jumps on the surface under the true gravity of that world (Moon 1.62, Mars 3.71, Titan 1.352 m/s²). On Venus, Jupiter and Saturn, where it is impossible to land, the guided tour presents the spacecraft that explored those worlds. There are 15 spacecraft models altogether: the lunar module of Apollo 11, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Surveyor, Sojourner, Ingenuity, Opportunity, Curiosity, InSight, Phoenix, Venera 13, Magellan, the Vega balloons, the Galileo probe, Cassini and Huygens. Each spacecraft has a guide called ORBIT telling its history, an animated short video showing what it did, and a question to test the comprehension. Each vehicle is tagged with the category: lander, rover, orbiter, flyby or atmospheric probe.

Benefits and expected results. This project turns complex history of space missions into an interactive story so that the learner discovers spacecraft types, how gravity varies from one world to another, and the achievements of each mission. We expect this experience to help learners get attached to long-forgotten robotic explorers and take interest in ongoing missions.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Three.js for 3D; Canvas for animated explainers; Web Audio API for generated sounds; the speech synthesis of the browser for ORBIT’s voice. No installation required, it works in the browser on desktop and mobile devices. We used Claude (Anthropic) as our AI assistant for programming, texts and graphics.

Creativity. The player becomes the explorer, who launches, cruises, lands, walks, jumps and meets the machines. Each machine is presented by a different 3D model, not the same model with a new name.

What factors did we consider? First of all, we had to keep scientific accuracy by not inventing the landing sites, dates, discoveries and landing missions to gas giants. We targeted schoolchildren as our audience and used clear language and labels. For accessibility we included keyboard controls, a voiced guide and a toggle to turn off the sound.
